extracted.intended_audience: readers of 18th‑century comic fiction; writers and students interested in stylistic examples and rhetorical devices
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of an excerpt from Laurence Sterne's Tristram Shandy (comic, digressive 18th‑century prose) with attention to the author's embedded stylistic and rhetorical observations. Useful for literary study or writers seeking period rhetorical techniques and informal style guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim: combine wit and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: When I sat down, my intent was to write a good book; ... taking care only, as I went along, to put into it all the wit and the judgment (be it more or less) which the great Author and Bestower of them had thought fit originally to give me
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states as a primary goal that a successful work should incorporate both wit and judgment. This is presented as an intentional principle guiding composition and tone; the ideal is a balance rather than an exclusive emphasis on either quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify understanding before applying an argument
rubrics_metrics.description: An illustration is no argument — nor do I maintain the wiping of a looking‑glass clean to be a syllogism;—but you all ... see the better for it — so that the main good these things do is only to clarify the understanding, previous to the application of the argument itself
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use illustrative examples to prepare and clarify the reader's mind before presenting formal argumentation. Illustrations help remove 'motes' or obscuring matter so the subsequent argument can be better grasped. The entry distinguishes clarifying devices from formal proof but values their pedagogical role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'set dissertations' and tall opaque words
rubrics_metrics.description: I hate set dissertations — and above all things in the world, ’tis one of the silliest things in one of them, to darken your hypothesis by placing a number of tall, opake words, one before another, in a right line, betwixt your own and your reader’s conception
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not obscure the reader with long, pretentious vocabulary or formal dissertations that interrupt comprehension. Prefer accessible phrasing; avoid piling obscure words between the reader and the idea you wish to convey (anti‑pattern: pretentious verbosity that blocks meaning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete household objects as illustrative aids
rubrics_metrics.description: for what hindrance, hurt, or harm doth the laudable desire of knowledge bring to any man, if even from a sot, a pot, a fool, a stool, a winter‑mittain, a truckle for a pully, the lid of a goldsmith’s crucible, an oil bottle, an old slipper, or a cane chair? — I am this moment sitting upon one. Will you give me leave to illustrate this affair ... by the two knobs on the top of the back of it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer ordinary, tangible images to explain abstract points. Concrete, familiar objects can make subtle distinctions visible and immediately comprehensible; the author models this by using the two knobs on a chair to embody wit and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the preface modest; let the work speak for itself
rubrics_metrics.description: NO, I’ll not say a word about it — here it is;—in publishing it—I have appealed to the world—and to the world I leave it;—it must speak for itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid grandiose prefatory claims or lengthy self‑justifications. A modest preface (or minimal prefatory commentary) that places the book before readers and allows the text to 'speak for itself' is preferred to overblown introductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit and judgment should go together (neither alone is satisfactory)
rubrics_metrics.description: You see, they are the highest and most ornamental parts of its frame — as wit and judgment are of ours — and like them too, indubitably both made and fitted to go together ... would any man ... have turned a piece of work out of his hand in such a condition? — would any man ... think, rather than be as it is, that it would be ten times better without any knob at all?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues (with the chair knobs metaphor) that wit without judgment, or judgment without wit, is defective; both are complementary and should be present in good writing. Anti‑pattern: showcasing one quality in the absence of the other, producing imbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match wit/judgment distribution to context and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: That of these two luminaries so much of their irradiations are suffered from time to time to shine down upon us, as he, whose infinite wisdom ... knows will just serve to light us on our way in this night of our obscurity ... the fervent wish in your behalf ... was no more than the first insinuating How d’ye of a caressing prefacer
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the amount and type of wit and judgment appropriate for expression vary by context, culture, and necessity. The author observes an uneven, providential distribution of such qualities and implies writers should proportion their use to the occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on external trappings or imposture to claim authority
rubrics_metrics.description: This has been made the Magna Charta of stupidity ever since — but your reverences plainly see, it has been obtained in such a manner, that the title to it is not worth a groat: — which by‑the‑bye is one of the many and vile impositions which gravity and grave folks have to answer for hereafter. ... I write not for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using outward signs (e.g., 'great wigs', 'grave faces') or deliberate imposture to suggest wisdom or authority. Genuine substance should trump performative signs of gravity; do not manipulate appearances to feign competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the rhetorical device of delayed naming/occlusion for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a singular stroke of eloquence ... not to mention the name of a thing, when you had the thing about you in petto, ready to produce, pop, in the place you want it. ... Otherwise, when a state orator has hit the precise age to a minute — hid his BAMBINO in his mantle so cunningly ... and produced it so critically ... it has done wonders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ strategic withholding (not naming something explicitly while alluding to it) to create dramatic or rhetorical effect. The passage praises the art of producing a concealed object at the right moment as a powerful oratorical tactic; guidance includes careful timing and physical concealment as a metaphor for rhetorical surprise.
